三个模块从不同角度支持 DDR 分组：

This appendix validates the causal predictive power of DDR features through three complementary analyses: permutation importance, Granger causality, and feature intervention.

\paragraph{Permutation Importance.}
Table~\ref{tab:perm-importance} reports the mean F1 drop when each feature's values are randomly shuffled across the test set (baseline F1\,=\,0.771).
Drifting features dominate: their average F1 drop (0.187) is $5.3\times$ larger than the near-stationary average (0.034), confirming that location-shift features---not shape features---drive depth classification.

\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{llcr}
\toprule
\textbf{Feature} & \textbf{Group} & \textbf{Mean F1 Drop} & \textbf{Rank} \\
\midrule
hapax\_ratio  & Drifting      & 0.235 & 1 \\
entropy\_mean & Drifting      & 0.170 & 2 \\
ttr           & Drifting      & 0.156 & 3 \\
entropy\_max  & Near-stat.    & 0.070 & 4 \\
entropy\_std  & Intermediate  & 0.057 & 5 \\
entropy\_min  & Near-stat.    & 0.019 & 6 \\
tail\_decay   & Near-stat.    & 0.014 & 7 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Permutation importance (6-gen LOGO). Each feature is shuffled independently; the resulting F1 drop quantifies marginal importance. Drifting features average $0.187$ vs.\ near-stationary $0.034$ ($5.3\times$).}
\label{tab:perm-importance}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Granger Causality.}
Table~\ref{tab:granger} reports Fisher-combined $p$-values from panel Granger causality tests (lag\,=\,1) across 8 generators ($N$\,=\,29{,}095).
Six of seven features exhibit significant Granger causality ($p < 0.001$), meaning past feature values predict future depth beyond what past depth alone explains.
The sole exception is entropy\_min ($p$\,=\,0.375), providing additional evidence for its near-stationary classification: it carries neither large marginal importance (Table~\ref{tab:perm-importance}, rank 7) nor temporal predictive direction.

\bottomrule

This appendix validates the causal predictive power of DDR features through three complementary analyses: permutation importance, Granger causality, and feature intervention.

\paragraph{Permutation Importance.}
Table~\ref{tab:perm-importance} reports the mean F1 drop when each feature's values are randomly shuffled across the test set (baseline F1\,=\,0.771).
Drifting features dominate: their average F1 drop (0.187) is $5.5\times$ larger than the near-stationary average (0.034), confirming that location-shift features---not shape features---drive depth classification.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{llcr}
\toprule
\textbf{Feature} & \textbf{Group} & \textbf{Mean F1 Drop} & \textbf{Rank} \\
\midrule
hapax\_ratio  & Drifting      & 0.235 & 1 \\
entropy\_mean & Drifting      & 0.170 & 2 \\
ttr           & Drifting      & 0.156 & 3 \\
entropy\_max  & Near-stat.    & 0.070 & 4 \\
entropy\_std  & Intermediate  & 0.057 & 5 \\
entropy\_min  & Near-stat.    & 0.019 & 6 \\
tail\_decay   & Near-stat.    & 0.014 & 7 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Permutation importance (6-gen LOGO). Each feature is shuffled independently; the resulting F1 drop quantifies marginal importance. Drifting features average $0.187$ vs.\ near-stationary $0.034$ ($5.5\times$).}
\label{tab:perm-importance}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Granger Causality.}
Table~\ref{tab:granger} reports Fisher-combined $p$-values from panel Granger causality tests (lag\,=\,1) across 8 generators ($N$\,=\,29{,}095).
Six of seven features exhibit significant Granger causality ($p < 0.001$), meaning past feature values predict future depth beyond what past depth alone explains.
The sole exception is entropy\_min ($p$\,=\,0.375), providing additional evidence for its near-stationary classification: it carries neither large marginal importance (Table~\ref{tab:perm-importance}, rank 7) nor temporal predictive direction.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Feature} & \textbf{Combined $p$} & $\boldsymbol{\Delta R^2}$ & \textbf{Significant} \\
\midrule
entropy\_std  & $< 0.001$ & 0.031 & Yes \\
hapax\_ratio  & $< 0.001$ & ---   & Yes \\
ttr           & $< 0.001$ & ---   & Yes \\
entropy\_mean & $< 0.001$ & ---   & Yes \\
entropy\_max  & $< 0.001$ & ---   & Yes \\
tail\_decay   & $< 0.001$ & ---   & Yes \\
entropy\_min  & $0.375$   & ---   & No  \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Granger causality (Fisher combined across 8 generators, lag\,=\,1, $N$\,=\,29{,}095). $\Delta R^2$ is reported where available.}
\label{tab:granger}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Key Findings.}
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
\item \textbf{Drifting dominance.} The $5.5\times$ permutation-importance gap confirms that drifting features (entropy\_mean, ttr, hapax\_ratio) are the primary depth signal carriers, consistent with the DDR partition derived from convergence analysis (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).

\item \textbf{Entropy\_min lacks causal direction.} Beyond its small effect size (F1 drop\,=\,0.019), entropy\_min is the only feature without significant Granger causality ($p$\,=\,0.375). This strengthens the near-stationary classification: the feature is neither marginally important nor temporally predictive.

\item \textbf{Entropy\_max asymmetry.} Entropy\_max ranks fourth in permutation importance (F1 drop\,=\,0.070) but produces the largest degradation in the counterfactual intervention ($-$2.0\,pp), indicating that it provides unique signal not redundant with other features---its causal contribution exceeds its marginal importance.

\item \textbf{Mistral heterogeneity.} In per-generator Granger tests, Mistral-7B shows non-significant hapax\_ratio and ttr ($p > 0.4$), though Fisher combination across generators remains significant. This generator-specific attenuation partly explains Mistral's lowest LOGO F1 (0.605) and suggests that DDR fingerprints are weaker in models with heavier repetition penalties.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

The central finding is that recursive generation alters \emph{where} the token-level surprise distribution sits but not \emph{how} it is shaped: autoregressive sampling with fixed top-$p$ plausibly truncates the conditional distribution at a consistent shape regardless of input, while mean surprisal systematically decreases as the model conditions on its own increasingly typical outputs.
Permutation importance, Granger causality, and feature intervention analyses confirm that DDR features carry causal predictive power beyond correlation: drifting features contribute $5.3\times$ more to classification than near-stationary ones, and 6/7 features exhibit significant Granger causality across generation depths, with entropy\_min as the sole exception (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-causality}).
This asymmetry is not intrinsic to recursion but parameter-dependent: at $t{=}1.0$, the location signal collapses ($\rho$ from $-0.60$ to $-0.002$; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}), and semantic-preservation constraints attenuate drift (elaboration F1\,=\,0.730 vs.\ continuation 0.781; Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}), consistent with \citet{broken_telephone}; cross-type transfer remains viable (F1\,=\,0.753).

Several boundary conditions constrain practical applicability.
Document-level gen-1 per-class F1\,=\,0.63 is insufficient for automated filtering but sufficient for corpus-level flagging ($O(1/\sqrt{n})$ error scaling); the primary difficulty is distinguishing gen-1 from gen-2+, consistent with DDR producing the smallest location shift at the first recursive step (86\% false negatives; Appendix~\ref{app:error-analysis}).
Cross-temperature transfer degrades when test-time temperature exceeds training ($t{=}0.7 \rightarrow 1.0$: overall 3-class F1 drops from 0.789 to 0.723; the most affected single generator, Qwen3-1.7B, drops to per-generator F1\,=\,0.418; Appendix~\ref{app:cross-temp}); depth fingerprinting assumes matched or lower temperature.
These patterns hold across reference model families (F1 within 0.013; Table~\ref{tab:cross-ref}).

DDR occupies a distinct position among recursive generation phenomena.
Model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse} describes irreversible degradation from \emph{retraining} on model outputs; inference-chain drift operates in a different regime where parameters are fixed, drift is fully reversible, and shape features are affected an order of magnitude less.
This divergence has practical implications: model collapse remediation focuses on restoring tail coverage, while inference-chain contamination preserves shape and thus requires location-based detection---a strategy that DDR directly enables.
Three depth classes represent the practical resolution ceiling (5-class F1\,$\approx$\,0.50; Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}), though richer representations recover substantially more signal (QLoRA F1\,=\,0.905; Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}).
Instruction-tuned models show attenuated fingerprints (OLMo-Instruct LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 vs.\ 0.763 base), but QLoRA on instruct data (F1\,=\,0.89--0.91 vs.\ XGBoost 0.58--0.73; Appendix~\ref{app:instruct}) indicates instruction tuning reorganizes rather than eliminates the signal, though this is demonstrated under within-model CV only; cross-generator instruct transfer (XGBoost LOGO F1\,=\,0.487) remains weak.

Adding Gemma-2-2B reduces the mean 3-class LOGO F1 from 0.770 (8-gen) to 0.751 (9-gen), a drop of $\Delta = -0.019$.
